title: How do you hear your own name across a noisy room?
hook: You tune out the chatter around you, until someone says your name.
summary: Sound you’re ignoring is still partly processed, which is why your own name can grab you from across the room.

cardBlocks.text: At a crowded party, most people can follow a single conversation and tune out the rest. Even so, if someone across the room says your name, you usually notice. That suggests ignored sound isn’t simply thrown away: one proposal is that the brain sorts through everything it hears without our awareness and picks out what matters.

The effect was defined and named in 1953 by Colin Cherry, who studied how people separate two messages heard at once. In 1959, a researcher named Moray asked volunteers to repeat a message played into one ear and ignore the other ear, where their own name appeared. About a third heard their name, a result repeated in 1995.
Sound you ignore is still partly processed, which is why your name cuts through a noisy room.

deepDiveBlocks.text: In the 1950s, air traffic controllers received messages from many pilots over the same loudspeaker. Hearing so many voices mixed together made the job very hard, and problems like this sparked much of the early research on attention.
The effect works best with both ears. People who hear with only one ear tend to be much more distracted by background noise.

claims.text: The effect was defined and named by Colin Cherry in 1953, who studied how people separate two messages heard at once.

support.excerpt: The effect was first defined and named "the cocktail party problem" by Colin Cherry in 1953.
Cherry conducted attention experiments in which participants listened to two different messages from a single loudspeaker at the same time and tried to separate them

claims.text: In 1959, Moray had volunteers repeat one ear’s message and ignore the other, where their name appeared; about a third heard their name, a result repeated in 1995.

support.excerpt: Moray (1959) used a dichotic listening task in which participants shadowed (repeated) the relevant message presented to one ear, and had to ignore the irrelevant message in the other ear, into which their name was inserted.
bout one-third of the participants reported hearing their name in the unattended channel, a finding replicated by Wood & Cowan (1995).
approximately one third of the participants report hearing their own name being presented in the irrelevant message during a selective listening task (Moray, 1959; Wood & Cowan, 1995).

claims.text: In the 1950s, air traffic controllers got messages from many pilots over one loudspeaker, which made the job hard and prompted early attention research.

support.excerpt: In the early 1950s much of the early attention research can be traced to problems faced by air traffic controllers. At that time, controllers received messages from pilots over loudspeakers in the control tower. Hearing the intermixed voices of many pilots over a single loudspeaker made the controller's task very difficult.

claims.text: The effect works best with both ears; people hearing with one ear are more distracted by noise.

support.excerpt: The cocktail party effect works best as a binaural effect, which requires hearing with both ears. People with only one functioning ear seem much more distracted by interfering noise than people with two typical ears.
